title: 22. Interview: Strong Consistency
summary: Interview Q&A for Strong Consistency — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Strong Consistency interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Define linearizability and explain why consensus is the only way to achieve it in a distributed system.
**Answer:** Linearizability is the property that every operation appears to execute atomically at a single real-time point between invocation and response, producing a total order that respects real-time precedence — i.e., if operation A completes before B starts, then B must observe A's effect. To provide this across replicas, the replicas must agree on (a) a single value for each write and (b) a single total order of all writes. That agreement is exactly the consensus problem, which the FLP impossibility result shows cannot be solved in a fully asynchronous network with even one crash failure while guaranteeing both safety and liveness. Real systems therefore use protocols like Raft or Paxos that rely on timeouts to detect failures and elect leaders, accepting brief availability gaps in exchange for safety. The implication is fundamental: linearizability and consensus are equivalent in cost — you cannot get one without paying for the other — which is why strong consistency is expensive and why engineers reach for weaker models whenever the application tolerates staleness.
**Visual:**
```
client1  --write(x=5)----commit@t1-->|
client2                          |   --read(x)-->
                                 v
        must see x=5 (real-time order respected)
        => requires consensus on commit point
```

### Q2. Compare Raft and Multi-Paxos. Why did etcd, Consul, and CockroachDB choose Raft?
**Answer:** Both protocols provide linearizable replicated logs via a leader-based quorum; both have the same fault-tolerance bound (tolerate f failures with 2f+1 nodes). The differences are pedagogical and operational. Raft was explicitly designed for understandability: leader election, log replication, and safety are decomposed into three sub-problems with clear invariants, and the paper includes pseudocode that fits on one page. Multi-Paxos is more general — it does not prescribe a single leader, allows for reconfigurations and prepares optimization phases — but it is notoriously hard to implement correctly because the paper leaves many details unspecified. etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV, and Redis Cluster's failover all chose Raft because its clarity reduces bug surface area and makes formal verification tractable (etcd's Raft has been model-checked extensively). Google's Spanner and Chubby chose Multi-Paxos because they predate Raft and the engineering investment in their own Paxos variants was already made. For a new system today, Raft is the default choice unless you have a specific need that Paxos uniquely addresses.
**Visual:**
```
Raft:        leader election + log append + safety (3 sub-problems)
             -> readable paper, formal models, single leader
Multi-Paxos: prepare/accept phases, leader optional, reconfig built in
             -> more general, harder to verify
```

### Q3. What is the role of leader leases, and how do they enable fast linearizable reads?
**Answer:** A leader lease is a time-bounded grant from a quorum of followers to the leader asserting that no other leader can be elected during the lease window. With an active lease, the leader knows it is still the leader and can serve linearizable reads locally without a quorum round-trip — cutting read latency from a full RPC to a local memory read. Without leases, every linearizable read must either (a) round-trip a quorum-read to confirm freshness, or (b) piggyback on the leader's heartbeat round to confirm it still holds quorum, both of which add latency. Spanner uses TrueTime-bounded leases (typically 10s) to provide linearizable leader reads globally. etcd's `serializable=true` is a slightly weaker variant — it returns the leader's local state without lease verification, which is faster but can return stale data within the lease window if the leader has actually been deposed. The trade-off is that leases must be shorter than the worst-case failure-detection window, otherwise the system can serve reads from a deposed leader — the so-called "stale leader" problem that TrueTime's bounded uncertainty solves.
**Visual:**
```
without lease:  read -> leader -> quorum round-trip -> ack -> return  (slow)
with lease:     read -> leader (lease valid) -> return locally        (fast)
lease expires:  read -> leader -> refresh lease via quorum -> return
```

### Q4. Why does Spanner need TrueTime, and what does "external consistency" mean?
**Answer:** TrueTime is Google's globally-synchronized clock API that returns an interval `[earliest, latest]` rather than a point, with the interval bounded to under 7ms using GPS and atomic clocks in every datacenter. Spanner needs it because pure linearizability only orders operations that overlap in real time; for non-overlapping operations (sequential writes from different clients in different DCs), linearizability is silent. External consistency — Spanner's term — extends linearizability to require that the order also respect wall-clock ordering of the *commit timestamps*, so that if transaction T1 commits before T2 begins in wall-clock time, T2's timestamp is greater than T1's. This is impossible with a normal clock because of skew: two DCs could each assign the same timestamp to different transactions. Spanner's commit-wait protocol assigns timestamps from TrueTime and waits until the uncertainty interval elapses before committing, guaranteeing that no later transaction can be assigned an earlier timestamp. The result is that reads can be served at a timestamp without coordination and still be externally consistent — a property unique to Spanner and central to its ability to provide serializable cross-DC transactions.
**Visual:**
```
TrueTime: now() = [t, t+epsilon]   (epsilon <= 7ms)
commit:   pick ts=t+epsilon, wait until now() > ts, then ack
                => no later txn can get ts < this one
                => external consistency
```

### Q5. A three-node Raft cluster has a slow disk on one follower. How does this affect write latency, and what mitigations exist?
**Answer:** Raft commits as soon as a quorum acks — for a three-node cluster, that is the leader plus one follower. A slow-disk follower simply falls behind; the leader commits with the healthy follower and the slow one catches up later via `AppendEntries` backoff. Write latency is therefore *not* directly affected in the steady state, but two secondary effects bite. First, the slow follower's log diverges over time, so when it eventually needs to catch up the leader must send large batches, consuming bandwidth and slowing the leader's `AppendEntries` pipeline. Second, the cluster is now one failure away from losing quorum — if the healthy follower also fails, the cluster cannot commit and stops accepting writes (CP behavior). Mitigations: monitor follower's `match_index` lag and alert when it exceeds a threshold (typically thousands of entries or seconds); configure `raft-log-replication-batch-size` to amortize the catch-up cost; consider removing the slow follower from the voter set via configuration change (Raft supports joint-consensus reconfiguration) and adding a healthy replacement; and ensure disks are provisioned with enough IOPS for the Raft log's fsync pattern (one fsync per commit, which can dominate latency on spinning disks). Production etcd clusters commonly pin Raft logs to NVMe for this reason.
**Visual:**
```
leader (fast disk) ---commit at quorum---> client acked
follower A (fast disk) --ack--> ok
follower B (slow disk) --lag--> catch up later

if A also dies: no quorum, write refused  (CP fail-closed)
```

### Q6. Compare linearizable reads, serializable reads, and stale reads. When is each appropriate?
**Answer:** Linearizable reads always return the latest committed value, requiring either a quorum round or a valid leader lease — appropriate for correctness-critical reads (balance after transfer, configuration value just changed, lock just acquired). Serializable reads (in the etcd sense) return the leader's local state without lease verification, which is faster but can return stale data within the lease window if the leader has actually been deposed — appropriate for reads where a sub-second staleness is invisible (dashboard, monitoring, internal config cache). Stale reads return any replica's state, including lagging followers — appropriate for read-heavy workloads where staleness is acceptable (search index, recommendation feed, public catalog). The cost gradient is steep: linearizable reads pay one quorum RTT (~1ms in DC), serializable reads pay nothing extra (~0.1ms), stale reads can hit any replica in any region (~0.5ms cross-region but reads scale horizontally). The architect's job is to default to the cheapest read that meets the invariant and escalate per-query when needed. etcd, CockroachDB, and Spanner all expose all three knobs; the cost of always using the strongest is wasted latency and reduced throughput for no business value.
**Visual:**
```
linearizable : quorum round / valid lease      ~1ms    correctness-critical
serializable : leader local, no lease check    ~0.1ms  tolerant of sub-s staleness
stale        : any replica, any lag            ~0.5ms  scale reads horizontally
```

### Q7. What is leader-election storm, and how do production Raft deployments mitigate it?
**Answer:** A leader-election storm is a positive-feedback loop where network jitter or slow disk causes followers to time out the leader, start elections, fail to reach quorum, time out again, and repeat — leaving the cluster without a stable leader for an extended period. The result is a cluster that refuses writes (CP fail-closed) even though every node is technically alive. Mitigations fall into three buckets. First, tune `election-timeout` to be at least 10x the worst-case RTT in the deployment (etcd default is 1s, but cross-DC deployments may need 5s+). Second, use pre-vote (Raft 2 extension) where candidates first check whether they could win an election before incrementing their term — this prevents a partitioned node from disrupting the cluster on reconnect. Third, isolate the Raft traffic on a dedicated network or QoS-marked queue so that user traffic spikes do not delay heartbeats. Production deployments also add monitoring on `raft_term` increases per minute — if it climbs above zero in steady state, the cluster is having elections and on-call should investigate. The right mental model is that Raft is robust to *failures* but fragile to *jitter*, and jitter is what production clusters actually experience.
**Visual:**
```
steady state:   leader heartbeats every 50ms, election-timeout 1s  (stable)
jitter spike:   follower misses 20 heartbeats -> starts election
                no quorum -> retries -> other followers start too -> storm
fix:            pre-vote, longer election-timeout, dedicated network
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You run a ticketing platform on etcd for inventory counts. A flash sale causes 50k writes/sec to the same key. etcd cluster falls over. Diagnose and redesign.
**Answer:** etcd is not designed for high write throughput on a single key — its Raft log serializes all writes to the same key, so a single hot key caps throughput at the leader's append-fsync rate (typically 10–20k writes/sec on NVMe, far less on spinning disk). The fix is to shard the inventory across many keys so writes parallelize: instead of one `ticket_count:event_42` key, use `ticket_count:event_42:shard_0` ... `shard_99`, and have clients randomly pick a shard to decrement. On read, sum all shards. The trade-off is that reads now need 100 keys instead of one, but reads are far less frequent than the flash-sale writes. A second optimization is to move inventory to a purpose-built system: Redis Cluster with Lua scripts for atomic decrement at 100k+ ops/sec per shard, or a CockroachDB cluster with sharded tables. etcd should remain the configuration store (small data, high write rate across many keys), not the inventory store. The mistake was treating etcd as a generic KV store; it is specifically a coordination store, and using it for hot data violates its design intent.
**Visual:**
```
hot key in etcd:   ticket_count:event_42  -> 10k w/s max (Raft serializes)
sharded:           ticket_count:event_42:shard_{0..99}  -> 1M w/s aggregate
                       (each shard is its own Raft group)
or move to Redis Cluster with Lua atomic decr (100k+/shard)
```

### Q2. A fintech runs its ledger on a three-node Raft cluster in a single region. The SRE team reports 99th-percentile write latency spikes to 200ms during nightly backups. What is happening and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The likely cause is fsync contention: Raft commits require fsync of the log entry to disk, and nightly backups saturate the disk's IOPS, pushing fsync latency from 1ms to 200ms. The leader cannot commit until the local fsync completes, so the entire write path is gated on disk latency. Fixes, in order of impact: (1) move the Raft log to a separate NVMe device dedicated to it, so backup I/O cannot contend; (2) run backups on a follower replica with `pg_start_backup`-style snapshot rather than reading from the live log device; (3) if the workload tolerates it, batch writes through a write-ahead buffer that batches multiple writes per fsync (this is etcd's `batch` mode, trading a small durability window for much higher throughput); (4) add a fourth node and use a quorum-of-three, so the leader can commit even if one follower is slow due to backup. The structural fix is to recognize that Raft write latency is dominated by `fsync` latency, and any other I/O on the same disk is a latency risk. The SRE team should alert on `commit_duration` and treat any p99 above 10ms as an incident.
**Visual:**
```
nightly backup reads saturate disk IOPS
   -> Raft fsync waits behind backup reads
   -> commit_duration p99 jumps 1ms -> 200ms
fix: dedicated NVMe for Raft log; backups read from follower snapshot
     + alert on commit_duration p99 > 10ms
```

### Q3. Google Spanner is used for AdWords billing. A billing transaction commits in region us-east, but 50ms later a read in region europe-west returns the pre-commit value. Is this a bug? Explain.
**Answer:** No, this is the expected behavior under Spanner's default isolation — Spanner provides external consistency for *transactions*, meaning a transaction T2 that *starts* after T1 *commits* will see T1's effect, but a read that was issued concurrently with or before T1's commit may not. The key question is whether the europe-west read's timestamp is greater than T1's commit timestamp. If the read is a stale read at a past timestamp (e.g., a read at `now() - 1s` for analytics), it correctly does not see the just-committed transaction. If the read is a strong read at the current timestamp, Spanner's commit-wait guarantees that by the time T1 returns "committed" to the client in us-east, the TrueTime uncertainty interval has elapsed and any subsequent read at `now()` in any region will see it. The 50ms gap in the question is ambiguous — if the read started *before* T1's commit completed in us-east (which includes the commit-wait), the read is correctly excluded. If the read started *after* T1's ack to the client, it is a bug and should be reported. The architect's mental model: external consistency is a property of transaction *start* and *commit* timestamps, not of wall-clock issuing times.
**Visual:**
```
T1: us-east write -> commit_ts = t1, commit-wait until now() > t1 -> ack @t_ack
read R in europe-west:
  if R.start_ts > t_ack  -> must see T1 (external consistency)
  if R.start_ts < t_ack  -> may or may not see T1 (correct)
strong reads use max(now()); stale reads use now()-X for analytics
```

### Q4. HBase strongly consistent per region, but your analytics team reports that a row inserted via `Put` is invisible to a `Scan` started in a different RegionServer 100ms later. What is the issue?
**Answer:** HBase is strongly consistent for reads and writes routed to the *current* RegionServer for a region, but a `Scan` started before the row was inserted can return a snapshot view that excludes the new row, because scans in HBase use MVCC read-points — a scan captures a `readPt` at start and only sees cells with `mvcc <= readPt`. If the scan started before the Put committed, the Put's MVCC number is greater than the scan's readPt and the row is correctly invisible to that scan, even though a new scan would see it. This is not a consistency bug — it is multi-version concurrency control providing snapshot isolation. The fix is to either (a) start the scan after the Put commits (use `Put` synchronously and wait for ack), or (b) for analytics that must see the latest state, use a fresh scan with no readPt constraint, or (c) for cross-region consistency, route through Phoenix or a SQL-on-HBase layer that handles the snapshot coordination. The lesson is that "strongly consistent" in HBase means linearizable per region, not serializable across long-running scans — those are different properties, and analytics workloads must account for the MVCC snapshot semantics.
**Visual:**
```
scan-1 starts at t=0, readPt=100
Put at t=50, mvcc=101, commits at t=80
scan-1 continues at t=100 -> only sees cells with mvcc <= 100 (excludes Put)
new scan-2 at t=200 -> readPt=102 -> sees the Put
(HBase is linearizable; scans are snapshot-isolated)
```

### Q5. ZooKeeper is used for leader election in your Kafka-like system. During a GC pause on the ZK leader, three participants each think they are the leader. How does ZK prevent split-brain on GC resume?
**Answer:** ZooKeeper uses Zab, which like Raft requires a quorum to elect and a quorum to acknowledge writes. During the GC pause on the ZK leader, the followers time out and elect a new leader — this requires a quorum of followers agreeing, so only one new leader can be elected. The participants in your system each create an ephemeral znode with sequence number; the participant with the lowest sequence number is the leader. If a participant is GC-paused, its ZK session may expire (the ephemeral node disappears), and a new participant takes over. The key invariant is that ZK guarantees only one participant can hold the lowest-sequence ephemeral node at any time, because ephemeral node creation is a Zab-committed write. On GC resume, the old leader's ZK client discovers its session expired and must re-register with a new (higher) sequence number, so it cannot retain leadership. The split-brain risk is at the *application* layer — if your leader does not check its ZK status before acting, it can act as a stale leader. The pattern is to fence every leader action with a ZK-issued fencing token (the znode's version or sequence number) that downstream services reject if they have seen a higher token.
**Visual:**
```
ZK leader GC pauses -> followers elect new ZK leader (quorum required)
participant P1 was leader (ephemeral znode seq=1)
P1's ZK session expires -> znode seq=1 deleted
P2 (seq=2) becomes seq=1 (lowest) -> new leader
P1 resumes -> session invalid -> must re-register as seq=3
P1's writes to downstream rejected (fencing token stale)
```

### Q6. You migrate a PostgreSQL-based accounts service to CockroachDB. The team is shocked that throughput drops from 30k to 8k writes/sec. Explain and propose a path forward.
**Answer:** CockroachDB provides serializable, linearizable transactions across a globally-distributed cluster — that is a much stronger guarantee than PostgreSQL's default (read committed on a single primary). Every transaction in CockroachDB goes through Raft consensus per range, paying at least one round-trip per write even within a region, and cross-region transactions pay additional round-trips for the transaction coordinator's intent resolution. The throughput drop is the cost of the stronger guarantee. The path forward has three parts. First, design the schema for locality: co-locate rows that are accessed together by using interleaved tables or regional-by-row partitioning, so most transactions touch only one range and one region. Second, reduce transaction scope: avoid long-running transactions that hold locks, batch independent writes, and use `AS OF SYSTEM TIME` for stale reads where possible. Third, scale out horizontally: CockroachDB's throughput scales roughly linearly with the number of ranges, so increasing the node count and partitioning the hot keys will recover throughput. The team should accept that 8k writes/sec on a 3-node cluster is the floor for strong-global consistency; getting back to 30k will require either more nodes or moving non-critical features to a weaker-consistency store.
**Visual:**
```
PostgreSQL single primary:     30k w/s (no consensus, single region)
CockroachDB 3-node, regional:   8k w/s (Raft per range, +1 RTT/write)
path forward:  +interleaved schema (locality)
              +regional-by-row partitioning (cross-region isolation)
              +scale nodes horizontally (per-range parallelism)
              +stale reads for non-critical paths
```

### Q7. A three-node etcd cluster experiences a 30-second network partition isolating the leader. Describe the timeline of events and what clients observe.
**Answer:** At t=0 the partition isolates the leader from the two followers. The leader stops receiving acks from followers, so it can no longer commit writes (no quorum) — any client write to the leader returns an error or times out. Meanwhile the two followers, who form a quorum among themselves, time out the leader's heartbeats (after `election-timeout`, typically 1–2 seconds) and elect a new leader. From this point (t≈2s) until the partition heals (t=30s), writes to the new leader succeed and are committed via the follower-quorum; writes to the old leader fail. Clients routed to the old leader get errors; clients routed to the new leader succeed. At t=30s the partition heals. The old leader discovers its term is stale (via `AppendEntries` response from the new leader) and steps down, reverting any uncommitted entries from its log. The new leader brings the old leader up to date by sending the missing entries. Crucially, no committed entry is lost because Raft's safety invariant requires the new leader to have all committed entries from the previous term. Clients see a ~2s window of write unavailability and possibly some retried writes, but no correctness violation — the price of CP.
**Visual:**
```
t=0:   partition isolates leader L0 from followers F1, F2
t=0-2: clients -> L0: writes fail (no quorum)
       clients -> F1/F2: writes fail (no leader)
t=2:   F1, F2 elect L1 (quorum = 2 of 3)
t=2-30:clients -> L1: writes succeed
        clients -> L0: writes fail (L0 still thinks it's leader)
t=30:  heal. L0 sees higher term from L1, steps down, reverts uncommitted
       L1 backfills L0 with missing entries
       no committed entry lost (Raft safety)
```
